reference.title: A boring weekend? Don’t tell anybody!
reference.text: A survey shows that 20% of British people tell lies about their weekend on social media. When people see their friends’ posts, they feel jealous, so they invent details about their own weekend. They want something to talk about on Monday at work or school. The most popular lies: going to a party or going away for the weekend; 3% even put on fake tan on Sunday night. People aged 18 to 24 lie most, and men lie more than women.

tasks.context: Bob1972: New York for the weekend, amazing! #greatweekend #nosleep. UrbanJ: Spent all day Sunday at work, then in bed at 9.00. #terribleweekend. Topsy: Husband took me to Paris for lunch on Saturday! #bestdayout. Betty: Sunday in the park with the family, picnic and games. #ilovesummer. — A boring weekend? Don’t tell anybody! A new survey has shown that 20% of British people tell lies about their weekend on social media. The survey, by a travel website, shows that people invent stories to make their lives appear more interesting than they really are. Psychologist Judi James, one of the organizers of the survey, said, ‘When some people read their friends’ posts and see their photos on Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, they begin to feel jealous of them. They think that their friends are having a much more exciting life. So they invent details about their own weekend.’ One of the main reasons people give for inventing these stories is to have something to talk about on Monday morning at work or at school. This is because they don’t want other people to think that they have a boring life. The most popular lies people tell are that they went to a party or went away for the weekend, and 3% of people even put on fake tan on Sunday night to make their colleagues think they’ve had a weekend away in the sun. One person in ten invents a romantic break with their partner. People aged 18 to 24 are the ones who most often tell lies on social media and men lie more often than women. Only 20% of people interviewed said that they always told the truth in posts. Judi James said: ‘Social media is becoming increasingly important in our lives, and it seems we’re living one life online and another in reality.’ So when you are feeling jealous on a Saturday night because your best friend is having a romantic dinner with her boyfriend in Venice, stop and ask yourself, ‘Is she really there, or is she just sitting at home feeling bored like me?’

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). It’s Monday morning. You have just read an article about people who tell lies about their weekend on social media. Ask the student, one at a time: What do you usually answer when people ask you ‘Did you have a good weekend?’ Is it always true? When was the last time you had a really exciting weekend? What did you do? Do you post photos of your weekend on social media? Do you think your friends’ posts are always true? Share your own answers briefly (you usually say ‘Not bad, thanks’; your last exciting weekend was a trip to the mountains last month). If the student makes a mistake with the past simple, repeat the correct form naturally.

Interview the student about last weekend with these questions, one at a time: Friday – Did you go anywhere exciting on Friday night? Saturday – Did you do anything in the house (cleaning, etc.) on Saturday morning? Did you go shopping? Did you buy anything? Did you need to work or study? What did you do on Saturday night? reference.title: Rules
reference.text: some- words go with a + verb (and in offers and requests: Would you like something to drink?). any- words go in questions and with a − verb. no- words go in short answers or with a + verb. any- + a + verb = it doesn’t matter which: You can come any day. Anybody can come to the party. I can sleep anywhere. You can bring anything.

reference.wrong: I didn’t do nothing last night.
reference.right: I didn’t do anything last night. / I did nothing last night.
reference.why: Don’t use two negatives: not + anything, or nothing + a + verb.

reference.title: File 3
reference.text: be going to + infinitive for plans (I’m going to look for a job) and predictions (I think it’s going to rain). Present continuous for future arrangements: What time are you leaving tomorrow? Defining relative clauses: who for people, which for things, where for places: He’s the man who lives next door. Is that the shop which sells Italian food?

reference.title: File 4
reference.text: Present perfect (have / has + past participle) for recent actions and news, with yet, just, already: Have you made your bed yet? I’ve already seen this film. For experiences with ever / never: Have you ever been to Africa? Details and finished times → past simple: When did you buy those shoes? Last week. something / anything / nothing, somebody / anybody / nobody, somewhere / anywhere / nowhere.

tasks.instruction: Can you understand this text? Read the article. How many different ways of making new words are mentioned?
tasks.note: Revise and Check 3&4 «Can you understand this text?» a → Blank; MODEL (6 способов; слова для новых технологий можно считать седьмым — принимаем 6 и 7)
tasks.context: 900 new words in 3 months. Everyone knows the English language is changing. Every three months the OED (Oxford English Dictionary) publishes updates to its online dictionary. One recent update contained 900 new words, new expressions, or new meanings for existing words. But where do they all come from? New words are created in many different ways. We can make a new word by combining two words, like gastropub (gastronomy + pub) or vlog (video + blog). Sometimes we put two words together in a new way, for example road rage or selfie stick. We also find that nouns can change into verbs. Take the word text. Text was always a noun (from about 1369, according to the OED), but it is now very common as a verb, to text somebody. Other new words already existed but with a different meaning. For example, tweet was the noise that a bird makes, but now we use it more often (as a verb or a noun) for a message that people put on the social networking site Twitter. Another way in which we make new words is by ‘adopting’ words from foreign languages, like barista or latte (imported from Italian when coffee bars became really popular in the UK in the 1990s). A lot of new words come from the names of brands or companies, for example we Skype each other and we google information. We also need more general words to describe new technology or new gadgets: wi-fi, ringtone, and smartphone are some examples. The invention of new words is not a new phenomenon. The word brunch (breakfast + lunch) first appeared in 1896, newspaper (news + paper) in 1667, and English speakers started to use the word café (from French) in the late 19th century. The difference now is how quickly new words and expressions enter the language and how quickly we start to use and understand them.

exercises.explain: Combining two words, putting two words together in a new way, nouns into verbs, new meanings for old words, words from foreign languages, brand names (and new words for new technology).

tasks.instruction: Can you say this in English? Talk about yourself
tasks.note: Revise and Check 3&4 «Can you say this in English?» (6 пунктов «Can you…?», самопроверка) → один разговор с ИИ по всем пунктам

exercises.situation: A friendly revision chat in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) after Files 3 and 4. Check that the student can do these things, one by one, with short questions and reactions: 1) talk about three plans for next month using going to, and make three predictions (e.g. about the weather or a match); 2) say three arrangements for tomorrow using the present continuous; 3) use paraphrasing to explain these words: a tweet, a gastropub, a selfie stick (It’s a kind of…, It’s something you use to…, It’s a place where…); 4) say three things they have already done or haven’t done yet today; 5) ask you three questions about your experiences using ever and answer yours (answer briefly, then ask a past simple follow-up); 6) say three sentences using something, anywhere and nobody. Keep it natural, one question at a time; if the student makes a mistake with going to, the present continuous, relative clauses, the present perfect or past simple, or something / anything / nothing, repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Show what you can say after Files 3 and 4.
